title: Sharps: handling, containers and injury response
audience: Cleaning staff who empty bins, clean equipment, or find sharps in patient areas and waste.
learningOutcomes: Describe the safe handling rules for sharps during cleaning and disposal.
Explain the container and placement rules for used single-use sharps.
Sequence the first-aid and reporting steps after a sharps injury.

instruction.heading: Where sharps injuries happen
instruction.body: Sharps injuries can happen during procedures, while scrubbing used instruments, when binning needles and when moving sharp tools after a procedure. The guideline wants care at every one of those points, since the risk spans the whole job rather than the procedure alone.

instruction.heading: Handling rules
instruction.body: Use an instrument, never bare fingers, for needles, tissue retraction and blade loading or unloading. Announce a sharp as it changes hands. Avoid hand-to-hand transfer: set the sharp down in a tray or a designated safe area. Round-tipped blades are preferred where the procedure allows. Minimise handling. Do not recap, bend or break a needle after use.

instruction.heading: Binning single-use sharps
instruction.body: Whoever used a single-use sharp is responsible for binning it at once in an approved container positioned where the sharp was used. Containers need clear labels, must resist punctures and leaks, and meet the Australian standards the guideline names. Never let one go above the three-quarter line. Keep them beyond children's reach and fixed or wall-mounted so they cannot topple. Reusable sharps being sent for reprocessing travel in a lidded, puncture-resistant container.

instruction.heading: Safety-engineered devices
instruction.body: Devices with built-in protection, such as guarded syringes and blades with covers, lower the injury risk. The current NHMRC guideline is dated 2019. Where a facility chooses them, it must back them with training.

instruction.heading: After an injury
instruction.body: Seek care without delay after a sharps injury. Where skin is broken, wash the site promptly with soap plus water or, lacking water, use alcohol rub. Avoid squeezing. Alert your supervisor at once and ask what aftercare, such as post-exposure prophylaxis, applies; it is most effective when started early. File an incident report with date, time, mechanism and, if known, the source person. The guideline notes that few exposures become infections, and fast action lowers the chance further.

procedure: Use instruments, not fingers, to handle any sharp you find or move.
Pick up a broken or loose sharp with forceps or a scraper, never by hand, and drop it into a sharps container.
Put used sharps straight into the approved container at the spot of use, never above the three-quarter line.
Never recap, bend or break a needle.
If you are injured, wash at once, do not squeeze, and get care immediately.
Report to the supervisor and complete the incident report with the required details.

workedExamples.situation: You are emptying a waste bin in a treatment room and find a used needle lying on top of the bags.
workedExamples.reasoning: Lift it with forceps or a scraper into an approved container and report it so the source can be tracked. If the needle has pierced your skin, start the injury steps at once.

equipmentAndPpe: Heavy-duty gloves for bin work, with puncture-resistant sleeves where the facility requires them
Forceps or scraper for loose sharps
Approved sharps container placed at the spot of use
Soap, water and a waterproof dressing for first aid

commonErrors.error: Reaching into a bin with a bare hand.
commonErrors.prevention: Look for sharps before reaching in; lift items out using the facility's method.

commonErrors.error: Recapping a needle to make disposal easier.
commonErrors.prevention: Never recap, bend or break a needle. Dispose of it as it is.

commonErrors.error: Filling a sharps container past the marked line.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop at the three-quarter mark and replace the container.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Gloves reduce the blood on a sharp's outer surface, yet they do not stop a sharp that goes through the glove. Gloves are not a sharps control.
Sharps containers stay out of children's reach and are fixed so they cannot tip.
Do not squeeze an injury site, and seek care immediately. Timing matters for post-exposure follow-up.

qualityStandard: No sharp is picked up by hand, and no needle is recapped, bent or snapped.
Each used sharp is placed in an approved container at the spot of use.
Injury response steps are followed in order and reported.
documentationEvidence: Sharps container change record with date and container location
Sharps injury or near-miss incident report with date, time, circumstances and source person if known
summary: Handle sharps with instruments, pass them safely, and never recap, bend or break needles.
Bin single-use sharps where they were used, in a labelled container filled only to the mark.
After an injury: wash, do not squeeze, seek care, report and complete the incident report.

knowledgeChecks.question: What must you do with a needle you find loose in a bin?
options: Pick it up with your fingers, because it is quick today
Move it with forceps or a scraper into a sanctioned sharps bin.
Recap it and place it in the general rubbish once it is cool
Leave it and tell nobody and carry on with the bin round at once

knowledgeChecks.question: How full should a sharps container be filled?
options: To the very top, to avoid waste at all
Not above the marked three-quarter line.
Until the lid can no longer close.
Half full, so it is less likely to tip.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the first step after a sharps injury that breaks the skin?
options: Squeeze the area to draw out any blood and then wash it with the cloth in the sink
Rinse the site at once with soap plus water, or an alcohol rub where water is absent.
Hold off telling anyone until the shift is over and carry on with the work
Apply a strong disinfectant directly to the wound and then cover it for the day
